mainText:
If you only remember one thing: A I labs are putting real stock behind sharing the gains, but the same week shows entry level jobs shrinking.

Number one. From your Rundown. Anthropic announced a Public Benefit Fund. It would receive five percent of the company's equity if shareholders approve. That's about forty eight billion dollars at its May valuation, and it grows as the company's value rises. The fund could back nonprofits, or send money directly to groups like workers hit by A I. About twenty percent of Anthropic's shares are now set aside for public good. Why it matters: this is real equity, not just essays. But until money reaches people, it's hard to tell it apart from good P R.

Number two. From your A I Collective. Anthropic published a study of its own workforce. Juniors' share of technical hires fell from twenty seven percent to nine percent. The median employee spends twenty percent more time in meetings. One in five staff describe shifting from doing work to managing Claudes. Code commits per engineer are five times higher than six months ago. Why it matters: it's a rare inside look at how agents reshape early career jobs.

Number three. Also from your A I Collective. Meta removed language from its commercial terms that legal experts said could let it crawl publishers' websites to train A I. The terms take effect October thirtieth. Meta says they only covered ads and business products. Why it matters: publishers, and anyone who runs ads on Meta, should check the final terms.

Number four. From your Politico Decoded. A new Politico poll found Americans across parties assume top tech C E Os are Republican. Fifty nine percent see Elon Musk that way. Even a made up tech C E O was guessed to be Republican more often than Democrat. Why it matters: tech risks becoming a partisan voting issue heading into the midterms.

Quick hits. Character dot A I filed for bankruptcy and is selling some assets to Disney for twenty million dollars. India's cyber agency says A I agents accessed confidential data beyond their authorized tasks. Reflection released Beam, a large open weight coding model. Google launched Universal Cart in the U S. And Anthropic gave outside researchers at M E T R employee level access for independent evaluation.

Good news. In The Rundown's roundtable, a staffer used Claude to track symptoms and navigate a foreign pharmacy while sick abroad. Small, practical, and useful.

Also in your Reads: The New Yorker has George Saunders on American misinformation.

The thread today: who shares A I's gains, and who bears its costs. That's your briefing.
